Welcome toSame Line, Two Stars

Two stars at 5800 K, one ten times larger: which shows the broader calcium line?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: pressure broadening set by surface gravity, g = GM/R2, in a main-sequence star and a giant of the same temperature

About this simulation

On screen
The calcium line at λ0 = 422.67 nm as Fλ/Fc against Δλ from −200 to +200 pm: the main-sequence star (1 M_⊙, 1 R_⊙) in the accent colour, the giant in solid grey, with dots at the half-depth points. A dotted line marks the line centre and a faint dotted line half depth. The inset in the lower right draws both stars to one scale on a dark sky, in the colour of a 5800 K blackbody.
Controls
The giant's radius, 5 to 25 R_⊙, and its mass, 1 to 4 M_⊙. The main-sequence star is fixed at the Sun's mass and radius.
Measured
g = GM/R2 for each star; the pressure where the line forms is g × 40 kg m-2, so Pgiant/PMS = ggiant/gMS. Each line is e−τ with τ a Voigt profile (thermal Doppler core, collisional Lorentzian wings), the same number of absorbing atoms in both stars and no natural width. W1/2 is the full width at Fλ/Fc = 0.5, found by bisection on the drawn profile.
Model limits
Both stars share one temperature and one number of absorbing calcium atoms, so only the pressure differs. The pressure is g times a fixed column mass, so P ∝ g; in real atmospheres the opacity also depends on the pressure and P grows more slowly, roughly as g2/3, but the ordering is the same. Collisions are with hydrogen atoms at one fixed cross-section, and there is no natural width, rotation or turbulence.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Which line is broader

Set the giant's radius to 10 solar radii and its mass to 1 solar mass, as the page opens. Before looking at the plot, predict which star has the broader line.

2 · Pressure in the giant's atmosphere

Keep the settings of question 1. The readouts give surface gravities of 274 m s−2 for the main-sequence star and 2.74 m s−2 for the giant. Before reading the pressure readout, predict the pressure in the giant's atmosphere as a fraction of that in the main-sequence star's.

3 · Growing the giant

Set the giant's radius to 5 solar radii and keep its mass at 1 solar mass. Before dragging the radius up to 10 solar radii, predict what happens to the giant's line.

4 · An even larger giant

Keep the mass at 1 solar mass and the radius at 10 solar radii. Before dragging the radius on up to 25 solar radii, which lowers the pressure more than six times further, predict the width of the giant's line.

5 · A heavier giant

Set the giant's radius to 10 solar radii and its mass to 1 solar mass. Before raising the mass to 4 solar masses, predict what happens to the giant's line.

6 · The most compact giant

Set the giant's radius to 5 solar radii and its mass to 4 solar masses, the most compact and heaviest giant the sliders allow. Before looking at the plot, predict how its line compares with the main-sequence line.

7 · Telling a giant from a dwarf

At one temperature, the width of pressure-broadened lines measures the surface gravity g = GM/R2. Giants have radii tens of times the Sun's but masses only a few times larger, so their gravity is far lower and their lines far narrower.

This is the basis of the MK luminosity classes, from V for main-sequence dwarfs to I for supergiants: stars of the same spectral class are told apart by the widths of their lines.

01

At a glance

This sim draws the calcium line at 422.67 nm in two stars of one temperature, 5800 K: a main-sequence star like the Sun, and a giant whose radius and mass you set. It reads out the surface gravity, the pressure ratio and the width of each line.

What you'll learn

  • How to read a line profile: the centre, the half-depth points and the width.
  • How a star's mass and radius set its surface gravity.
  • How the giant's line responds to its radius and its mass.
  • How line widths connect to the luminosity classes.
The plot axes, before any line is drawn, and the two stars to one scale.

What's on screen

  • Accent-colour line: the main-sequence star, fixed at 1 M⊙ and 1 R⊙.
  • Grey line: the giant. A dot marks where each line crosses half depth.
  • Dotted lines: the vertical one marks the line centre, the faint horizontal one half depth.
  • Inset and sidebar: both stars drawn to one scale, then the controls and the readouts.
See itLook at the two lines at the opening settings. Watch for: the dotted centre line, the half-depth line, and the dot where each line crosses it.

Fixed: both stars are at 5800 K, with the same number of absorbing calcium atoms and no natural width. The main-sequence star is always 1 M⊙ and 1 R⊙.

03

Core and wings: the core is the same, the wings follow the pressure

Calcium atoms move at random, and this thermal motion smears the line into a Gaussian core. At one temperature that core is the same in every star. Collisions with other particles shift the atomic energy levels and add damping wings, which fall off as the inverse square of the distance from the line centre (notes 3.4).

The sim gives both stars the same number of absorbing atoms along the line of sight, so both lines are black at the centre. The flux is Fλ/Fc = e−τ, where the optical depth τ is a Voigt profile: a Gaussian core with collisional wings.

The calcium line in both stars at the opening settings: the giant at 10 R⊙ and 1 M⊙. Dots mark the half-depth points.
Key idea. The temperature sets the core and the pressure sets the wings. Here only the pressure differs between the stars.
See itCompare the two lines at the opening settings. Watch for: both lines black at the centre, and the grey line reaching 1 almost at once while the other is still well below 1 at ±150 pm.
04

Pressure and gravity: the pressure follows the surface gravity

The pressure at a level supports the weight of the gas above it. So it equals g times the mass per unit area of that gas, Σ, where g is the surface gravity (notes 3.1):

The sim's column is Σ = 40 kg m−2.

The light we receive escapes from about the level above which too little gas is left to absorb it. In stars of similar temperature and composition, that column Σ is similar. So the pressure is proportional to g, and the pressure ratio is the gravity ratio:

Equal columns of gas, over different gravity.

The main-sequence star has g = 274 m s−2. The giant at 10 R⊙ and 1 M⊙ has g = 2.74 m s−2, a hundredth of that, so Pgiant/PMS = 0.0100.

See itRead the two gravities and the pressure ratio. Watch for: g = 274 and 2.74 m s−2, and a ratio of 0.0100: 10 times the radius, 1/100 of the gravity.
05

Width and gravity: in the wings, the width goes as √g

Far from the centre the core has died away and the wing gives an optical depth that falls as 1/x² with the offset x. The half-depth points lie where τ = ln 2, so their offset grows as the square root of the damping width γL, and γL grows with the pressure:

W1/2 is the full width at half depth, found in the sim by bisection on the drawn profile.

For the main-sequence star the wing formula gives 104.1 pm and the sim reads 104.2 pm. With M from 1 to 4 M⊙ at R = 5 R⊙, the gravity rises fourfold and the width from 21.5 pm to 42.0 pm: a factor 1.95 rather than 2, because the core still adds a little.

R M

These sliders move the sim too, and follow it.

See itStart with a 5 R⊙ giant of 1 M⊙. Watch for: g = 11.0 m s−2 and a width of 21.5 pm.
See itNow raise the mass to 4 M⊙. Watch for: g four times larger, 43.9 m s−2, and the width at 42.0 pm.
06

A floor: the Doppler core stops the line narrowing

Growing the giant from 5 to 10 R⊙ at 1 M⊙ takes the width from 21.5 pm to 13.0 pm. From 10 to 25 R⊙ the pressure falls a further 6.25 times, to 0.0016 of the main-sequence value, yet the width only reaches 11.9 pm.

The giant's half-depth width at 1 M⊙, from the sim's line.

Once the damping is small, the wings no longer reach half depth and the Gaussian core sets the width. A saturated line has an optical depth at its centre of about 1000 in this model, so its black core is wider than the 3.6 pm Doppler width. The half-depth width of the core alone is:

σ = 1.55 pm is the Gaussian standard deviation; τ0 ≈ 1000 is the optical depth at the centre. This gives 11.8 pm.
Key idea. Lowering the pressure further cannot narrow the line below its thermal core. That floor depends on the temperature, the atoms and how many of them absorb, not on the pressure.
See itSet the giant to 25 R⊙. Watch for: the pressure ratio at 0.0016 but the width at 11.9 pm, hardly below the 13.0 pm of the 10 R⊙ giant.
07

Giants and dwarfs: the width of the line measures g

Stars of one spectral class have similar temperatures, so L = 4πR²σT⁴ makes the more luminous stars the larger. The 10 R⊙ giant here is 100 times as luminous as the 1 R⊙ star. Morgan, Keenan and Kellman used the narrower lines of such stars to define the luminosity classes: Ia and Ib supergiants, II bright giants, III giants, IV subgiants and V main-sequence dwarfs. The Sun is G2 V, Aldebaran K5 III and Rigel B8 Ia.

A giant's radius is ten or more times a dwarf's but its mass only a few times larger, so its g is lower by a factor of 100 or more. Mass and radius trade off through M/R²: 4 M⊙ at 10 R⊙ has g = 11.0 m s−2, the same as 1 M⊙ at 5 R⊙, and the same 21.5 pm line. Even the most compact giant here, 4 M⊙ at 5 R⊙, has g = 43.9 m s−2 and a line 42.0 pm wide, still short of the main-sequence 104.2 pm.

See itSet 4 M⊙ at 10 R⊙, then compare with 1 M⊙ at 5 R⊙. Watch for: g = 11.0 m s−2 and a width of 21.5 pm in both cases.
08

Where it matters

  • Distances. The spectral class and the luminosity class, read from the spectrum, give a star's absolute magnitude on a calibrated H–R diagram. With the apparent magnitude, that gives the distance of a star too far for a measured parallax (notes 3.1).
  • White dwarfs. They have their own class, D. Their radii are tiny, so their surface gravity is thousands of times the Sun's, far beyond this sim's range, and their lines are strongly broadened.
  • Stellar analysis. The surface gravity is measured from the wings of lines like these, alongside the temperature and the composition.
Go deeper: what the sim holds fixed

Both stars share one temperature and one number of absorbing atoms, collisions are with hydrogen at one fixed cross-section, and there is no natural width, rotation or turbulence. The column Σ is fixed, so the pressure is exactly proportional to g.

In real atmospheres the opacity also depends on the pressure, and P grows more slowly with g, roughly as g2/3. The ordering of the lines is the same.

09

Summary

In one line. At one temperature, the width of a spectral line measures the star's surface gravity g = GM/R², which is how a spectrum tells giants from dwarfs.

Key points

  • The pressure where the line forms is g times a fixed column of gas, so the pressure is proportional to g.
  • The wings widen as √g; the Doppler core sets a floor at about 11.8 pm here.
  • The radius counts squared in g, the mass only once.

Common mix-ups

  • "The same temperature means the same line." The cores match; the wings do not. The widths are 104.2 pm and 13.0 pm.
  • "A larger star has a thicker atmosphere, so a broader line." A larger radius lowers g as 1/R², and the line narrows.
  • "The line keeps shrinking with the pressure." At 25 R⊙ it reads 11.9 pm, not a few picometres.

Things to try on your own

  • Set R = 25 and raise M from 1 to 4: g rises fourfold, but W only from 11.9 to 12.5 pm.
  • Set M = 2 and R = 7: g = 11.2 m s−2 and W = 21.7 pm, close to R = 5 at M = 1.

The line profiles are Figure 23 of the notes.
